claims.text: Standard pre-exposure Q235 steel has a natural, non-uniform mixture of surface oxides and processing-related inclusions such as MnS.
Localized-corrosion initiation in chloride-containing environments is controlled by microgalvanic coupling between non-uniform inclusions and the ferritic matrix.
Microgalvanic coupling associated with inclusions interferes with formation of a continuous, adherent passive iron-oxide film.
Removing or passivating deleterious inclusions should suppress corrosion degradation at room temperature.
At moderately elevated temperatures, faster oxide-film formation may partially compensate for corrosion degradation.
Moderately elevated temperatures may promote oxide spallation.
Electropolishing or mild acid etching followed by inhibitor immersion can remove or chemically passivate MnS and other deleterious inclusions.
Removing or passivating inclusions promotes formation of a uniform, adherent iron-oxide passive layer.
Discrete inclusions in untreated Q235 steel act as local cathodic sites.
The resulting microgalvanic cells accelerate anodic dissolution of the adjacent ferritic matrix.
Inclusion-associated microgalvanic cells hinder formation of a coherent, protective passive iron-oxide film.
A continuous passive layer formed after inclusion removal or passivation limits localized corrosion.
At 25 °C, treated samples are predicted to have lower corrosion-current density than untreated samples.
At 25 °C, treated samples are predicted to have lower mass loss than untreated samples.
At 25 °C, treated samples are predicted to develop a more uniform and adherent passive film than untreated samples.
The anticipated room-temperature reduction in corrosion rate is greater than 20%.
At 60 °C, treated samples may initially corrode more slowly because of faster film formation.
Subsequent oxide spallation at 60 °C may diminish the treatment's corrosion-suppression effect.
The controlled study compares untreated and surface-treated Q235 samples in static 3.5 wt% NaCl at 25 °C and 60 °C for identical durations such as 72 hours.

Failure of treated samples to show statistically significant improvements, including at least 20% lower corrosion-current density and mass loss plus improved film uniformity, is specified as falsifying the proposed inclusion-controlled mechanism.
